edges.description: The knockout does not reproduce the combined respiratory chain deficiency. Complex assembly is unaffected and respiration falls only moderately.
edges.limitations: This is a negative result in a transformed human cell line, not in an affected organ. The disease's respiratory deficiency was measured in patient liver and muscle, both post-mitotic and both far more dependent on oxidative phosphorylation than a cultured line in glucose-containing medium. The model therefore cannot settle whether the architectural lesion is insufficient to cause the deficiency, or whether the cellular context needed to reveal it is missing - but it does mean the entry's chain from cristae collapse to combined deficiency is not demonstrated in the one system where the lesion is isolated.

nodes.description:
Several reported alleles, all loss of function and all removing the protein rather than altering it. The gene is small and every reported variant truncates it.
The founding allele is the homozygous frameshift p.(Gly15Glufs*75), in a consanguineous brother and sister. Later reports add a splice-site variant in C19orf70, the homozygous frameshift c.13_29del (p.Trp6Profs*71) which truncates within the first ten residues, and c.209dupT (p.Ala73Argfs*32), which removes the second RDSWN motif required for MIC13 function.
Fibroblasts from the c.13_29del patient have no detectable MICOS13, so these are true nulls rather than hypomorphs.

nodes.description:
The first cell line deleted for MIC13, made with CRISPR/Cas in human cells. Where the patient fibroblasts show the lesion sitting alongside the disease, a knockout in a clean genetic background shows that removing MIC13 is by itself enough to abolish cristae junctions.
This model also separates the entry's two mechanistic claims, and the separation is informative rather than tidy. Cristae junctions are lost completely and the assembly of MIC10, MIC26 and MIC27 into MICOS fails, exactly as in patients. Respiratory chain complex assembly, by contrast, is unaffected and respiration falls only moderately, so the model does not reproduce the combined respiratory chain deficiency that names the human disease. Either the human deficiency needs something this model does not have - an affected tissue, a developmental context, time - or the architectural lesion is not a sufficient cause of it.

nodes.description:
Multiple OXPHOS complexes are deficient at once, in liver and muscle. "Combined" is the diagnostic label and it is also the mechanistic clue: a defect in one complex's subunits or assembly factors affects that complex, whereas a defect in the membrane they all occupy affects all of them.
The strongest evidence that this is secondary to the architectural lesion rather than an independent problem is a rescue: expressing wild-type MICOS13 in the patient's own fibroblasts restored respiratory chain function.

nodes.description:
MICOS13 is a small subunit whose job is to build and hold together the rest of the complex. Its loss is therefore not the loss of one component among seven: a defined subcomplex comprising MIC10, MIC26, MIC27 and QIL1 fails to form.
In Kishita et al.'s patient the protein was directly shown to be absent from fibroblast mitochondria, so the assembly failure follows from protein loss rather than from a hypomorphic variant with residual function.
The founding report makes the selectivity sharper still. In those patients' fibroblasts both MIC13 and MIC10 were absent while MIC60 was present at normal abundance. MIC60 is the core of the other MICOS subcomplex, so what fails is one arm of the complex rather than the complex as a whole - which is a more specific claim than "MICOS is disrupted" and is consistent with the MIC10-MIC26-MIC27-QIL1 subcomplex loss reported independently.

nodes.description:
The structural lesion of the disease. Cristae junctions are the narrow necks that connect each crista to the inner boundary membrane, and they do two things: they hold the folded surface area on which respiratory complexes are concentrated, and they partition the intermembrane space so that the crista lumen is a distinct compartment. Contact sites link the inner membrane to the outer.
Losing them is therefore not simply a morphological finding. It removes the geometry that makes oxidative phosphorylation efficient, which is why an architectural defect presents as a bioenergetic disease.

nodes.description:
Reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number, found in Kishita et al.'s patient - the reason that group proposed reclassifying MICOS13 as a cause of mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome - and independently again in Ammar et al.'s patient six years later.
Two independent reports is what moves this from a single-patient observation towards a feature of the disease. It remains true that not every report measured copy number, so the denominator is the number who looked rather than the number who have it.
This is unusual for the gene class. Depletion syndromes are typically caused by defects in deoxyribonucleotide metabolism or in the mtDNA replication machinery, and MICOS13 is neither. The authors say so themselves. Whether cristae collapse causes depletion, or the two are parallel consequences of a failing organelle, is not established.

This is the experiment that makes the entry's central causal claim more than an association. Complementation in the patient's own cells controls for genetic background in a way that no comparison with unrelated controls can.
